program: Food access, social services and mental wellness

what: Nourishing Hope provides food, social services and mental wellness support to Chicago residents.
Its counselors offer intake and ongoing care, while case managers help with benefits, transit, housing and employment resources.
Food distribution and individual support address several connected barriers to household stability.
strengths: Current licensed clinical and case-management services establish a plausible mechanism.
Food and benefits access can improve usable household resources.
Multiple access routes serve residents facing practical barriers.
reservations: Food pounds and neighbors served are not additional therapy cohorts or causal outcomes.
Net food substitution, benefit access and clinical effectiveness are unmeasured here.
Whole annual costs and donated food do not establish marginal gift productivity.

sections.what: Nourishing Hope, EIN 36-2734184, operates food markets, delivery, social services and mental wellness in Chicago. Counseling is available to Chicago residents aged 14 or older after intake; alternative referrals and ongoing coordination are offered. Social services include benefits applications, transit, grant eligibility, housing and job-search support. The official donation route is current; no checkout transaction was tested.
sections.monitoring: The organization reports over six million food pounds and 50,000 neighbors in 2025. These are delivery measures, not unique additional therapy participants or avoided illness. Track unique households, additional usable food resources net of substitution, actual benefit receipt, session completion, clinical outcomes and process burdens. Existing SNAP, Medicaid, other food banks and public clinics remain alternatives. Food-service use is not required for social services.
sections.qualitative: A Cochrane review of primary-care counseling found modest short-term mental health advantages over usual GP care, but not long-term superiority or overall healthcare cost reductions. The evidence is dated and from different settings; it does not identify local treatment fidelity, adolescent effects or QALYs. The model's .04 utility increment for six months is a weak separate judgment. No mortality, ordinary survivor earnings or additional food-related clinical benefit is stacked on the same people.
sections.cost:
Original April–March annual recognized expense plus direct event expense gives FY2025 $20,399,467, FY2024 $19,122,654 and FY2023 $16,917,206; mean $18,813,109. Schedule D identifies no additional donated-service expense requiring a second addback. FY2024 reconciliation's $308,941 matches event cost and is counted once. Noncash contributions of $11,222,804, $10,791,364 and $8,878,798 are not automatically another expense added to already recognized food resources. Unrecognized volunteer opportunity costs remain unknown.

A judged 1,000 local household opportunities and .5 additional annual-work response expose 500 households. A .1 clinical share and .5 completion yield 25 clinical residents within the same union. Judged .04 utility for six months, quarter-year delay and 3% discount yield .496319 clinical QALYs. This is a narrow conditional bundled-services channel with the whole annual denominator, not complete portfolio EV or measured marginal-gift productivity.

Two hundred households conditionally gain $300 usable food purchasing resources and $600 benefits in one year, already net of alternative food, substitution, taxes, benefit withdrawal and replacement support. These are actual incremental resource hypotheses, not pounds times retail price or gross salary. Each positive component retains .5 for health overlap; full negatives remain. Full $75 process time/transport burden leaves $375. Three hundred other households lose $75. One welfare-equivalent person per household, $20,000 annual resources and one joint log yield 1.284554 equivalents. Additional family welfare is unpriced. Combined 1.780872 gives $114.547608 million per ten combined equivalents, not ten clinical QALYs.

Clinical failure preserves resource exposure and costs. Full-union harm, negative resources, payer loss and external care burdens are stresses. Public transfers and donated food need counterparty accounting; matched payer incidence is separate, not attenuated by recipient overlap. Central payer and external costs are unknown-neutral references, not factual zero or complete-world benefit.
sections.funding: Original government grants were $1,069,603, $1,018,888 and $406,011. Public benefits eligibility and food alternatives continue without this recipient. The .5 response judges additional annual funded work while retaining full annual expense; b=1 shows full response. Actual unmet expansion, alternative funding, food supply replacement and marginal donor response remain unknown.

model.geographicAttribution: Chicago resident households; one clinical resident in subset of resource union.
model.formula: exposed=N*b; clinical=exposed*clinicalShare*completion; Q=clinical*q*discounted finite years−full union harm. Positive-only overlap per signed food/benefit component, then joint household log once. Price=10*C/(health+resources).
model.counterfactual: Existing food banks, public benefits, clinics and alternative providers continue.
model.attribution: Throughput, additional funded-work response, therapy uptake, utility and usable resources are separate judgments.
model.uncertainty: Net substitution, unique additional cohorts, local clinical outcomes, outside incidence and marginal expansion unknown.
model.nativeOutcomes: Additional completed counseling with finite symptom-health area and signed net usable food/benefit resources.
